title: Scanning index - K. Fennimore, Marchfield Public Library
description: The list of what has been scanned out of the Marchfield library's microfilm cabinet and local collection, reel by reel and item by item, with what shape each one is in and how to ask for a copy.

blocks.body:
Marchfield Public Library, 114 Ward Street. This is the list of what has been scanned out of the microfilm cabinet and the local collection, with what shape each one is in.

The same list is on paper at the reference desk. The paper one gets written on first.

None of it searches. There is no OCR and no money for OCR, so every page is an image, and the name index is typed by hand. If you cannot find a thing, telephone and ask me and I will look.

I am at the desk Tuesday to Friday. The reader runs Tuesdays, Thursday mornings, and the hour before we open.

head: Count
rows: 205 of 291, and one of those is out of place
1911 to 1958. 1959 to 1962 is scanned and not indexed
15 cents a page. Looking is free

blocks.body:
Everything indexed is on the county wiki, free, with no account: [url=synth://wiki.gridfall.net/wiki/verity-county]wiki.gridfall.net[/url]. A year that is scanned and not indexed can still be had, but you have to give me a date rather than a name.

Batches go up on the library's own page when a reel finishes: [url=synth://marchfieldlibrary.blog/]marchfieldlibrary.blog[/url].

The newer wiki keeps an article on the substation fire. If you are reading [url=synth://verity.wiki/wiki/substation-fire-2003]that article[/url] and it gives 2004, you have caught it between edits; I put it back about twice a week. The document is item 41 on [url=/other]the other list[/url] and it is two pages long.

items: Tuesday 6 October 2026. Reel 205 added out of sequence with a note. Totals brought forward. Item 41 recounted.
Thursday 24 September 2026. Reel 204 finished.
Saturday 12 September 2026. W. Pennock's 2026 deposit received and receipted. Item 34.

blocks.body: This page sits on the old personal space at verity.net, which costs the library nothing and still works. If it stops working the list is still on paper at the desk.

291 reels, January 1911 to December 1998. A vendor filmed the bound set in 1983 and 1984 and typed an index card for every reel. The cards are in the drawer on top of the cabinet. The vendor stopped existing in 1994.

The bound set itself went in 1986, two years after the filming, which was ordinary practice then and is why the film is the only copy of most of this.

The run is complete except for four months of 1943, where the film is damaged. There is a note on that below the tables.

Scanning started in March 2016. It goes at about eleven pages an hour on a good day and about eight once the lamp is warm and I have to stop and let it cool. Same reader throughout. Tuesdays, Thursday mornings, and the hour before we open.

Page counts in the tables are pages actually scanned, not frames on the film. A blank frame still has to be turned past and it is not counted.

head: Reels
Covers
Pages
Condition
rows: Reel 4 is soft at the start. The first eleven frames of 1912 are a grey wash and there is no other copy of them anywhere I have found. From frame 60 it is good film.

Four pages to an issue for most of 1918. Two weeks of March 1919 are not on the film and were not in the bound set either; the vendor wrote MISSING FROM ORIGINAL on the card in pencil and he was right.
Splices at 39 and at 44. Both are the vendor's and both hold. Reel 41 runs out of focus for about 200 frames in the spring of 1922 and enlarges readable.
Good film all the way through. The page numbering restarts mid-week twice in 1927, which the paper did and the camera did not, and I have scanned it as printed.
Reel 71 has a tear repaired with tape that has gone brown. It runs. I run it slowly and I do not rewind it fast, and whoever has this job next should not either.
Someone has written on the card for 88 in biro: FILMED TWICE. It was not filmed twice. I have left the card as it is and put a note behind it saying so.
Wartime newsprint. It is grey, it scans grey, and there is nothing to be done about that at this end.
June to September 1943 is the damaged stretch. 62 issues, blistered, mostly a wash. See the note below. The rest of these two years is ordinary film.

Clean. The 14 June 1946 issue carries a sixteen-page supplement on the county roads with a fold-out map, and the map is wider than the frame, so it is filmed in three overlapping shots and I have scanned all three.
Reel 133 is out of order inside itself: the week of 12 August 1949 is filmed after the week of 26 August. Filmed as found and scanned as filmed. I have not renumbered anything and I am not going to.
Fine film. The last two frames of 151 are the camera operator's slate, and they are scanned, because they have a date on them and that date is the only record of when this part was done.

152 carries the courthouse fire: Friday 20 February 1953, page one, five columns, frames 1180 to 1196. The photographs on that page are the best pictures of the tower that exist, because the paper had to go and find one out of its own file.
Nothing wrong with these. Two of the cards are typed on a different machine, which is the only reason I looked at them twice, and they check out against the leaders.
178 stops at the end of March because the paper changes there. See the note below the tables.
186 sat half done for five weeks in the autumn of 2025 while the reader was out. It is September 1959 on both sides of the gap and you cannot see the join.
The paper is bigger from here and a reel holds less of it. 1960 took five and a half months to get through, against four months for 1958. That is the advertising and not the machine.
Good film. 203 finished on Tuesday 18 August.
Finished Thursday 24 September. Nothing wrong with it.

The card says January to June 1963. The leader says 1974 in the vendor's own typing and the frames say 1974 as well, so the film is right and the card is wrong. Scanned as found, 15 and 16 September, because it was threaded and somebody will want it.

Checked against the leader. Not scanned.

Not scanned. About 75,000 pages. I am pulling every tenth card and checking it against the leader, which is 29 reels and about two hours, and the result goes on [url=synth://marchfieldlibrary.blog/]the library page[/url] when it is done.

The six months reel 205 should have held. It is on a reel with a 1974 card on it, somewhere in the two hundred and forties, and I will find it when I get there. Until then do not ask me for anything between January and June 1963, because I have not got it.

blocks.body:
The Ledger printed Tuesdays and Fridays until Monday 31 March 1958 and six days a week from the next morning. The vendor's reels change with it, which is why reel 178 ends where it does and why a reel holds about a quarter of a year before that date and about two months after it.

This is also the answer to the question I get about why the early years went so fast. They did not go fast. There was less paper.

June to September 1943 is 62 issues of blistered film. Most of it is a grey wash. Some of it will come up if you enlarge one frame at a time and give it an afternoon, and I have done that for four issues that people asked for by date.

It was damaged before the vendor filmed it. I know that because his own card says FILM POOR JUN-SEP in pencil and because the damage is in the original image and not in the emulsion.

The bound set those four months came off went in 1986 with the rest. There is no other copy in this building. Two places worth trying are on [url=/elsewhere]the other page[/url] and one of them is a woman in Tessler with a scrapbook.

People write to ask why there is nothing about the county fair in those months. There is nothing because the fair did not run in 1943 or 1944.

Indexed: 1911 to 1958, by surname, giving the date and the page.

Scanned and not indexed: 1959 to 1962, and the 1974 reel.

Indexing is slower than scanning and cannot be done while a reel is running, so it happens when the machine is down or when somebody is at the desk who does not need me. 1954 to 1958 was done in five weeks in the autumn of 2025 while the reader was in pieces.

The index gives you a name, a date and a page. It does not give you the article, and it will not tell you which of the four Ludekes it is. Ask and I will look at the page and tell you.

400 dpi, grey, one page to a file, named by date and page. A page runs between 300 KB and 1.1 MB depending on how many photographs are on it. A year runs between 700 MB and 2 GB.

I will send you a page. I will send you a week. I will not send you a year; if you want a year, bring a drive to the desk and it takes about twenty minutes.

Sixty-one items are accessioned. Fifteen of them are scanned. The rest are on the shelf and can be read here, and I will take a thing out of turn if somebody actually wants it, which is the only reason half of these are done at all.

The numbers are accession numbers. They mean where the folder is and nothing else.

Nineteen issues out of a hundred and eight years, all of them arrived inside other people's boxes. The run itself is at Milbrook and is not filmed. See [url=/elsewhere]the other page[/url].
The Gridfall Ledger, paper file, unbound, in boxes
The issue of 14 June 2003 is not in the box and has not been since at least 2014. The 2009 boxes were wet at some point before they came to us and the bottom inch of that year is stuck together.
The Gridfall Ledger, 11 to 20 June 2003, out of the paper file
Scanned because people kept asking for one page of it. Page one of 12 June is the page they want: four columns and a photograph of the fence line at Depot and Quarry.
Scanned and not published. See below. The staples on 4 and 5 have rusted through the paper and those two are in sleeves.
Blue Kestrel material, copied for us by Marion Teale

Four menus, the booth map, nineteen photographs, and six pages in her own hand on the 1977 kitchen fire. The booth map is on the back of a placemat, and the placemat is wider than the scanner bed, so it is in two pieces with an overlap.
Photographed at the clerk's counter. Every page says TRANSCRIPT across the top and I have not cropped it off. See below.
Somebody paid $24.15 for these on a records request, took what he wanted out of them and left the rest on the desk on his way out. Request number 2026-018 is stamped on the first page.
Cooking at St Mark's, the Ladies' Aid, St Mark's Lutheran, Marchfield
Spiral bound. Cover detached and kept with it. Three recipes crossed out in biro and one of them has NO written beside it in the same hand.
The Cardinal, Verity Central High School yearbook
Pages 9 to 12 are missing. Cut out with a blade, close to the gutter. They are junior portraits, surnames K through R.
Folded in four for ninety years. The fold has gone brown and two of them have split along it and are in sleeves, folded, because unfolding them further would finish them.
This library's annual reports to the county, clipped from the Ledger
The 1934 one is page two of 18 August 1934. Circulation 14,206 volumes, 1,918 registered borrowers, $211.40 spent on books.
Carl Ordway's field notebooks, county weights and measures
Pencil, one line to an inspection: the date, the business, the scale, whether it passed. Pencil scans faint so I scan it slower, which is why four notebooks of eleven.
Carl Ordway's correspondence, a departmental newsletter, four photographs of the tannery yard

The photographs are undated. Two people have said what the long building on the left is, and both suggestions are in the folder in pencil with the name of whoever said it. I am not dating them off a caption I wrote.
W. Pennock's reception logs, 4.2190 MHz USB, paper and a disc
Deposited every September. The 2026 book came in on Saturday 12 September. See below.
A copy of boards.gridfall.net through 2012, on disc

Made by D. Carver and brought in without being asked. Copied to the drive in 2023 and read back in March, which is the whole of what looking after it amounts to. It reads on the office machine and on nothing else in this building.
The Milbrook VFW post's printed notice sheets, in a binder

They used to come off the wall after eight weeks and go in the bin. Now the sheet goes in a binder and the binder comes here once a year. It took four minutes to arrange and nobody had thought of it in nine years, including me.
State utility commission, summary of findings, Substation No. 3
Photocopy of a photocopy. The cause is one sentence and it is on page two. See below.
Bound, thick, and a directory scans badly flat. 1957 and 1968 are off the shelf and I would take either of them in any condition.
Came from three different people, one sheaf at a time. 1963 and 1964 are missing entirely and the 1958 numbers are duplicates of each other.

Given by the school in 2019 when they cleared the office. Half of them have no names on the back. Of the ones that do, two are in the wrong order left to right, which I know because two of the people are still living and told me.
Eleven boxes that came in without explanation
Not accessioned. Listed to the box and no further. See below.

blocks.body:
State utility commission, summary of findings, Gridfall Substation No. 3. November 2003. Two pages.

Photocopy of a photocopy. The header on page one is grey and the page numbers are written in by hand, not printed. The cause is one sentence on page two and it reads [i]insulation degradation consistent with age[/i].

The commission's investigation file is the commission's. It is not here and it is not the county's either, and the county clerk's office spends part of every month telling people that. This is the summary, which is public, and it is two pages, and anybody may have it.

I have written twice for a clean copy. I have an acknowledgement for each letter.

It is the item on this page that is asked for most often and it is the shortest thing in the building. Sixty-three copies have gone out since I started keeping the tally in January. Fourteen of those were people who had read somewhere that the cause was lightning and wanted to see the other version.

The Ledger's own report of the morning after is item 8: page one of 12 June 2003, four columns and the photograph of the fence line. That decade of the paper is also still on the paper's old site, which nobody maintains and which is the cleanest copy of it there is: [url=synth://verityledger.com/]verityledger.com[/url].

The Kestrel Letter, Nos. 1 to 26, February 2020 to August 2026. Four pages each, photocopied, folded and stapled. 104 pages.

This library subscribed at No. 3, so 1 and 2 are copies of a subscriber's copies from Coyne Flats and are a generation worse than the rest. No. 17 has a correction in Marion Teale's hand on page three, in pen, and I have left it in the scan.

Scanned and not published. She asked that it not go on the internet and I said that it would not, and that is the whole of the reason. You can read the run at the desk, and I will copy any issue for anybody who wants one. The box lives behind the desk rather than on the shelf for the same reason.

Her old site is still up and is better than anything anybody else has written about that diner: [url=synth://kestrel-journal.net/]kestrel-journal.net[/url]. It stopped in 2019 and it does not need adding to.

No. 26, August 2026, is four pages on the 1977 kitchen fire, which started in the fryer, and on the eleven days the place was shut, and on who lent them a grill. It is the only first-hand account of that week that exists in writing.

County commissioners' minutes, the typed transcripts, 1946 to 1958. 1,140 pages, photographed at the clerk's counter on Tuesday 9 and Tuesday 16 June with a camera on a copy stand, which is allowed there and costs nothing.

The bound volumes for those thirteen years were in the basement at 14 Depot Street in March 1994 and were damaged past saving. The transcripts were typed in 1996 and 1997 out of what could still be read and out of the county's own carbon copies. Roughly two thirds of the thirteen years survives in some form. What does not survive is described in writing, which is the right way to do it and is rarer than it should be.

Every page says TRANSCRIPT at the top. I have not cropped it off and nobody should, and anybody quoting from these should say so.

The record is the clerk's and this is a copy for the reading room. [url=synth://verityclerk.gov/s/minutes]Their page on the minutes[/url] is accurate and is better than anything I could tell you about them.

Cooking at St Mark's, the Ladies' Aid of St Mark's Lutheran Church, Marchfield. 1968. 96 pages.

Given by Gail Prine in June. It was her mother's and it had been in a kitchen drawer and then in a garage.

Three recipes are crossed out in biro and one of them has NO written next to it in the same hand. That page is scanned with the crossing-out on it. Somebody wrote that, and it is part of the book now.

214 names with an address under most of them, arranged by street. For 1968 that is a better list of who lived where in this town than anything the county has, and the county has nothing like it, and I have checked.

Church and grange cookbooks are worth bringing in for that reason and for no other. [url=synth://stmarks-verity.org/]St Mark's[/url] has its own bound bulletins from 1954 and those are worth a morning as well.

The Cardinal, Verity Central High School, 1961. 116 pages, 112 scanned.

Pages 9 to 12 are missing. They have been cut out with a blade, close to the gutter, and they are junior portraits, surnames K through R. I do not know who did it or when. The book came to us in 2013 out of a house clearance on Bellamy Street with four other books and a box of postcards.

This is the only yearbook in the collection. The district keeps its own set and does not lend them, which is reasonable and is also why there is one here.

If you have a yearbook from any year, I will scan it and give it back inside the week. That offer has stood since 2016 and has been taken up twice.

W. Pennock, Ashkettle. Reception logs, 4.2190 MHz USB, 2019 to date. On paper and on a disc, deposited every September.

Not scanned. The paper is legible, the disc copies onto the drive in about four minutes, and nobody has asked for a scan. If somebody does ask, it is about nine hundred pages of ruled columns and it will take me a fortnight, and I will do it.

The 2026 book came in on Saturday 12 September. He waited while I wrote the receipt and said he had not expected one.

His own pages carry the same figures and his method written out, which is more than most of what is published on the subject can say: [url=synth://pennock-sdr.net/]pennock-sdr.net[/url].

Eleven boxes that came in without explanation between 2009 and 2021. Not accessioned. Listed to the box and no further, in these words:

[list][*]Photographs, unnamed. One wedding, one railway, forty-one of a house.[*]A ledger of a business with no name anywhere in it. 1909 to 1931. Somebody was good at ruling lines.[*]Minutes of something, 1954 to 1961. Not the county. Nineteen members and a treasurer who resigned twice.[*]Hymnals, eight, water damaged.[*]A shoebox of funeral cards, most of them Coyne Flats.[*]Slides, two carousels, unlabelled.[*]Four boxes not yet opened past the top layer.[/list]

If one of these is yours, or was your father's, I would like to know what it is. What you know about a box is half of what the box is, and once it has come through the door without you, I cannot get that half back.

blocks.text: How to ask me for something

blocks.body:
Telephone the reference desk on 782-1170, Tuesday to Friday ten to six, Saturday ten to two. Or write to 114 Ward Street, Marchfield. Or come in.

The reader is free to use and I will thread it for you and show you how, which takes about a minute and a half and is not hard, only fiddly.

There is no account, no form and no charge for looking, and there never will be, because the day there is, it stops being a library thing.

items: A date. A date is best. With a date I can usually have it the same day.
Or a name and a range of years. Five years is a search. A year is a shelf and a decade is a project.
How the name might have been spelled by somebody else. Half the Kuhns in this county are Koons in 1931 and a third of them are Coons by the war.

Whether you want the article or the page. The article is four inches in the middle. The page is a whole broadsheet and carries everything that was next to it, which is usually the half people end up wanting.
Whether you are in a hurry. People do not say, and then they wait three weeks politely, and I would rather have known.

head: Cost
rows: Paper copy, oversize, done on the flatbed in two halves
Whatever it costs. People send stamps and stamps are fine
An account, a login, a membership
There is none and there will not be

items: A date, in a year that is scanned: the same day, or the next day I am in.
A name, in an indexed year, 1911 to 1958: two or three days.
A name, in a year that is scanned and not indexed, 1959 to 1962: about a week, and I will do it on a Thursday.
A name, in a year that is neither: I will tell you that, and tell you which reel it would be on, and you can come and turn it yourself, and I will thread it.
Anything before 1911: the film does not go back that far. See [url=/elsewhere]the other page[/url].
Send you a whole year. Bring a drive.
Read handwriting to you down the telephone. Photograph it and send the photograph and I will look at it properly.
Tell you what a document means. I will tell you what it says, and what page it is on, and the two are not the same job.
Look for records the county holds. Those are at the clerk's counter at 14 Depot Street and I will tell you which counter and what it costs there before you drive over.
Take a deposit with a condition on it that I cannot honestly keep. I will say so at the desk rather than afterwards.

blocks.body:
Cite the document and not me. The date, the page and the column, so that the next person can go and turn the same frame and see whether you were right.

If you want it formatted properly I will format it for you. Leave a note at the desk, or on my talk page on the wiki, and it takes me five minutes.

If you are correcting something somebody else wrote, cite it the same way and do not mention them at all. It works better and it is less trouble afterwards.

Requests go in a hardback book at the reference desk, one line each, with the date, what was asked for and whether it was found. It is the fourth book since 2016.

I keep it because it is the only list of what this collection actually gets used for. The most asked-for things this year, in order: obituaries, the substation fire summary, wedding announcements, house histories, and the 1974 fair.

If you asked me for something and never heard back, it is in that book and it is my fault, and telephoning again is not a nuisance.

entries.body: Is the 1974 reel going up or is it shelf only. I want 9 August 1974, the fair page, the one with the buckle advertisement in it.

entries.author: kfennimore
entries.body: It is up. Friday 9 August 1974, page 11, second and third columns, Fair Association, under the horse show entries. Solid brass, 500 struck, $6.00 at the Association table. It went up in the batch on the 18th.

entries.author: wpennock
entries.body: 204 at 358 pages and 205 at 402. If the rest of the sixties runs at 205's rate then your 75,000 is low by about 9,000 and the year at the end of it moves. Not a complaint. An estimate.

entries.author: kfennimore
entries.body: It is low. I used the last three years and not a good year, so the year at the end of it is low too. I will redo it when 1963 is finished and I will put both numbers up.

entries.author: mod_dcarver
entries.body: You said you would tell me when 204 was done. I found out by reading this page, which is fine, it is what the page is for. 204 is done.

entries.author: gail_prine
entries.body: My mother's cookbook is on a website. I did not expect that and I have looked at it four times. My sister in another state has looked at the page with the crossing out on it, which is the one she remembers.

entries.body: Item 20 should say which meetings it covers rather than the months, because the commissioners met twice in July 2003 and the second one is the one people want. Otherwise this list is better than the county's own and I have told them so.

blocks.text: What is not here, and who has it

blocks.body: People drive to Marchfield for things this library has never held. This is where those things actually are. I will telephone ahead for you if you want; three of these are one person and a key, and a Thursday afternoon is not a Tuesday morning.

head: What
Where
Note
rows: Deeds from 1841, commissioners' minutes from 1903, marriage records from 1889, the certified canvass
County clerk, 14 Depot Street, Gridfall, ground floor

[url=synth://verityclerk.gov/]Their own page[/url] is accurate. About 340 reels in two cabinets in the basement and a typed reel list on top of the left-hand one. It is eleven degrees down there in February. Bring a cardigan.

Not filmed and not scanned. All of 1918 is missing, most of 1943 and 1944, and issues scattered through. The binding on the older ones is going. [url=synth://verityhistory.blog/]Marjorie Hoberg[/url] worked out what survives and where, which nobody had done before and which took her two months. The paper's own site is the last few years only: [url=synth://milbrookgazette.com/]milbrookgazette.com[/url].

[url=synth://verityledger.com/]verityledger.com[/url]. It is the clean copy of that decade and it is better than our paper file, which has holes in it. Nobody looks after it and it has been up for eighteen years.
The paper does not keep a public archive of its own editions. What is on paper here for those years is item 6 and the 2009 boxes were wet.

[url=synth://verityschools.org/s/minutes-archive]Their archive[/url] goes back to 2001 and has five years missing out of the middle of it. The paper copies for those five years exist and are in the office, and somebody there will photocopy them if you ask in person.

Nobody has filmed any of them. [url=synth://stmarks-verity.org/]St Mark's[/url] has its bulletins bound from 1954 in the church library and will let you sit with them. Two people did that this year and both found what they came for.
The historical society, Depot Street, Gridfall
Thursday afternoons, and no website, and a telephone that is answered on Thursdays. It is worth arranging your week around. They have the tannery and the fairgrounds and we do not.

She does not use the internet and that is a decision she made and not a thing that happened to her. Her old site is at [url=synth://kestrel-journal.net/]kestrel-journal.net[/url] and it stopped in 2019. Items 12 and 15 here are copies she made for us herself, in 2004 and in 2011, and she would not take anything for either.
The board is still up and D. Carver pays for it out of his own pocket. The disc here is the copy of last resort and has never been needed, which is the point of a copy of last resort.
His figures and his method are written out on his own pages. The paper copy here is the same thing on paper, a year behind, and it is here because paper does not need anything to read it.

Mrs. Dwyer in Tessler has a scrapbook with clippings from that summer pasted in, some of them dated in pencil in her mother's hand. And the state library holds the Bowes City paper, which covered this county badly and covered it, which is better than the nothing I have.
Anything about somebody who is living

The index is a public newspaper and I will tell you what page a person is on. I will not tell you where they live now. I have been asked eleven times this year and the answer has been the same eleven times.

blocks.body:
The reel list on the cabinet at the clerk's office and the reel list on this site are not the same list and neither one is complete. Theirs is four typed pages that have not been retyped since 2004, with pencil additions in three hands. Ours is [url=/ledger]on the other page[/url] and is typed by me and is wrong in at least one place, which I know because reel 205 was wrong for forty-two years before anybody noticed.

If you want a year and it is not on theirs, telephone here before you drive over. If it is not on mine, telephone them. It costs a minute and it saves a morning.

items: Yearbooks. Any school, any year, back the same week.
Church and grange cookbooks. Any year. They are the best list of who lived where that exists.
Marchfield telephone directories for 1957 and 1968.
The Milbrook Gazette, any loose issue, particularly 1943 and 1944.
Funeral home registers, if the home has closed and somebody has the books.
Photographs with names written on the back, which is rarer than it ought to be and is the whole difference between a photograph and a box of faces.
